items.prompt:
(a) Plot these water-cooling measurements on the blank grid and draw an appropriate curve. Time/min: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Temperature/°C: 80, 72, 65, 59, 54, 50.

![Blank cooling grid](visuals/VIS-6117-12-02-learner.svg) [3]

(b) Calculate the average cooling-rate magnitude for the uninsulated water from 2 to 6 min using the data 72 °C at 2 min and 59 °C at 6 min. [2]

(c) State the instrument needed to measure the water temperature in this investigation. [1]

(d) Plan an investigation to compare two insulation materials by measuring how water cools. Decide what to keep constant, what to measure, how to repeat the experiment and how to reach a conclusion. Include safe handling of hot water. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Axes: time/min horizontally from 0 to 10, temperature/°C vertically over a suitable range such as 20–90. Plot (0,80), (2,72), (4,65), (6,59), (8,54), (10,50) accurately and draw a smooth decreasing curve through or close to the trend without unjustified oscillations. The answer panel is separate from the blank learner grid.

(b) Temperature decrease = 72 − 59 = 13 °C; interval = 6 − 2 = 4 min. Average cooling-rate magnitude = 13/4 = 3.25 °C/min. The signed temperature gradient is −3.25 °C/min.

(c) A thermometer or suitably calibrated temperature probe.

(d) Use identical vessels and 100 cm³ water portions, each starting at 80 °C. Fit equal-thickness jackets of the two materials with the same covered area and identical lids. Place them in the same 22 °C surroundings away from differing draughts. Position thermometer bulbs in the water without touching glass and record temperatures at fixed times, for example every two minutes for ten minutes. Repeat each arrangement and compare mean cooling curves or temperature drops; the smaller drop indicates better insulation under the test conditions. The teacher supplies the hot water, vessels stand on heatproof mats and handling avoids burns. Predict that a more effective jacket gives a smaller temperature fall.
marking_guidance: Part a: Suitable evenly scaled axes with both quantities and units (1).
Part a: All six points within ±1 °C vertically and appropriate horizontal plotting tolerance, normally half a small square (1).
Part a: Suitable smooth decreasing trend, not an arbitrary zigzag or oscillation (1).
Part b: Temperature change divided by elapsed time, 13/4 (1).

Part b: 3.25 °C/min as magnitude, or −3.25 °C/min clearly identified as signed gradient (1). Exact supplied-data answer is 3.25; accept 3.0–3.5 only when a permitted graph read-off is explicitly used, with follow-through.
Part c: Thermometer / calibrated temperature probe (1).
Part d: Same vessel and water volume (1).
Part d: Same starting temperature (1).
Part d: Vary material while controlling thickness/covered area/lids (1).
Part d: Record temperature at fixed times with suitable apparatus (1).
Part d: Repeat and control ambient conditions (1).
Part d: Compare cooling curves or drops for a conditional conclusion (1). Safety and a sensible prediction are expected supporting plan details; no invented extra marks.
